name: Taurus
introduction: is the Bull, among the oldest constellations: Mesopotamian astronomers knew it as the Bull of Heaven more than 4,000 years ago, when the Sun was in Taurus at the start of spring. The Bull charges at Orion, its face a V of stars with fiery Aldebaran as its eye and the Pleiades on its shoulder. It is best seen on northern winter evenings.

sections.title: What makes it special
paragraphs: Taurus contains the two most famous star clusters in the sky. The V-shaped Hyades, about 150 light-years away, is the nearest open star cluster to the Sun. The Pleiades, or Seven Sisters, about 440 light-years away, is a young family of hot blue stars currently drifting through a cloud of dust that reflects their light.
Aldebaran looks like the brightest member of the Hyades, but it is a coincidence of perspective. At 67 light-years, it is less than half as far away. The map lets you see this for yourself.

image.caption: Star View schematic · catalogue positions and distances to scale
image.alt: Aldebaran appears among the Hyades but is less than half as far away; the Pleiades are nearly three times farther than the Hyades.

sections.title: Notable stars
paragraphs: [Aldebaran](hip:21421) is an orange giant about 44 times wider than the Sun. The Pioneer 10 spacecraft is drifting in its general direction, though it would take about two million years to get there.
The Hyades giants [Prima Hyadum](hip:20205), [Ain](hip:20889) and [Chamukuy](hip:20894) trace the V. In 2007, Ain became the first star in an open cluster found to have a planet.

[Elnath](hip:25428) marks the tip of the northern horn and was once shared with Auriga. [Tianguan](hip:26451) marks the southern horn, and [Atlas](hip:17847) is one of the brightest Pleiades, named after the sisters’ father.

sections.title: Beyond the stars
paragraphs: The [Pleiades Nebula](id:pleiades-nebula) and [Hind’s Variable Nebula](id:hinds-variable-nebula) glow around young stars; Hind’s Nebula is lit by T Tauri, which gives its name to a class of newborn stars still settling down; many of them form in the nearby [Taurus Molecular Cloud](id:cahlon-cloud-22).

Near Tianguan lies the Crab Nebula, M1, the remains of a supernova recorded by Chinese astronomers in 1054. At its center, a pulsar spins about 30 times a second. In autumn, the Taurid meteors, debris from Comet Encke, radiate from Taurus.
